title: AI Assistance Reduces Persistence and Hurts Independent Performance
content:
Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence

Title:AI Assistance Reduces Persistence and Hurts Independent Performance
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:People often optimize for long-term goals in collaboration: A mentor or companion doesn't just answer questions, but also scaffolds learning, tracks progress, and prioritizes the other person's growth over immediate results. In contrast, current AI systems are fundamentally short-sighted collaborators -- optimized for providing instant and complete responses, without ever saying no (unless for safety reasons). What are the consequences of this dynamic? Here, through a series of randomized controlled trials on human-AI interactions (N=1,222), we provide causal evidence for two key consequences of AI assistance: reduced persistence and impairment of unassisted performance. Across a variety of tasks, including mathematical reasoning and reading comprehension, we find that although AI assistance improves performance in the short-term, people perform significantly worse without AI and are more likely to give up. These findings are particularly concerning because persistence is foundational to skill acquisition and is one of the strongest predictors of long-term learning. We posit that persistence is reduced because AI conditions people to expect immediate answers, thereby denying them the experience of working through challenges on their own. These results add to the growing literature on cognitive offloading and AI-induced deskilling, and suggest the need for AI model development to prioritize scaffolding long-term competence alongside immediate task completion.

report.summary: Randomized trials (N=1,222) show AI assistants boost short-term task performance but reduce persistence and worsen people's unassisted performance, raising fresh deskilling concerns.
report.background: The study lands in the middle of a fast-growing debate about cognitive offloading — the tendency to hand mental work to a tool rather than do it oneself. Earlier work has linked heavy GPS use to weaker spatial memory, and recent surveys of knowledge workers found that the more confidence people place in generative AI, the less critical thinking they apply. Programming has produced similar signals, with copilot users reporting discomfort when asked to work without assistance. What has been missing is causal rather than correlational evidence. This paper, revised six times on arXiv since April 2026, supplies it through randomized controlled trials, and frames the problem structurally: today's assistants are optimized to always answer instantly and completely, more like a vending machine than a mentor who scaffolds growth, tracks progress, and sometimes withholds the answer on purpose.
key_points: The authors ran a series of randomized controlled trials with 1,222 participants across tasks including mathematical reasoning and reading comprehension, allowing them to claim causal rather than merely correlational effects of AI assistance on how people learn and perform.

Short-term and long-term effects point in opposite directions. With AI available, participants performed better than controls. Once the AI was removed, the same people performed significantly worse than those who had never used it — a measurable impairment of unassisted skill.

Persistence dropped sharply. Participants who had worked with AI were more likely to abandon problems when the assistant was gone, and persistence is one of the strongest known predictors of long-term learning and skill acquisition.

The proposed mechanism is expectation, not laziness. Always-instant, always-complete answers condition users to expect immediate resolution, denying them the productive struggle of working through difficulty — the very experience that builds durable competence.

The authors argue current systems are 'short-sighted collaborators' and call for model development that optimizes for scaffolding long-term competence alongside immediate task completion, rather than treating the answer as the only product.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this reframes an uncomfortable trade-off: engagement metrics and satisfaction scores reward instant, complete answers, which may be exactly the design that erodes user capability over time. Expect more pressure to build and benchmark 'scaffolding' behaviors — hints, Socratic questioning, deliberate withholding — and to measure retention and unassisted performance rather than task completion alone. For developers, heavily copilot-dependent workflows carry real skill-atrophy risk, suggesting value in periodic no-assist practice and team norms about when to reach for the tool. For regular users, the practical takeaway is not abstinence but dosage: use AI to check reasoning after an attempt rather than to replace the attempt, or the tool quietly becomes a crutch that makes the underlying skill disappear.
report.tools: To follow this line of research, use alphaXiv for community discussion on the paper, Connected Papers or Litmaps to map the surrounding cognitive-offloading and deskilling literature, and Hugging Face Papers for related preprints. If you want to try scaffolding-first designs rather than answer-first ones, look at Khanmigo, Google's Gemini Guided Learning mode, ChatGPT's Study Mode, and Math Academy — all built around hints, questioning, and mastery tracking instead of instant solutions.
